Phylogeny of the catalytic core

Maximum-likelihood tree of the 2,062 tips: the 76 curated reference enzymes, drawn as squares in bold, and one representative sequence per sequence-homogeneous variant. Branch lengths are substitutions per site in the aligned Rieske-plus-catalytic core.

Not every variant has a tip, and the rule is two-ended. A variant with a single member is its own representative. A variant with 5 or more members contributes the medoid of its members. Variants in between, with two to four members, are skipped, because a medoid of so few sequences is not a stable choice. The consequence is measurable: 1,986 of 3,076 variants appear here, and the 1,090 that do not hold 2,844 entries, or 15 % of the database. Those entries are present everywhere else on the site; they have no tip on this tree. Four types have no representative at all under this rule (3NTDO, DxnA1), so they appear only as their reference square.
group 1group 2group 3group 4group 5 ungrouped curated reference
How to read this tree. A reference embedded in a tight clade of tips of its own colour is a type that is well sampled by close relatives, and its substrate label is informative for that clade. A reference on a long branch, or a clade whose tips are coloured for a different type than the nearest reference, marks a region where profile assignment and phylogeny disagree; there, type membership carries no functional claim. The colour blocks are not the historical RO groups, and this page used to claim they were. Whether each group forms a single clade is now measured on this tree rather than asserted. Among the 530 sequences whose assignment is neither distant nor novel, only 2 come out as single clades: group 5, with 95 of 95 leaves, and ungrouped (plant chlorophyll ROs: PAO, CAO, PTC52), with 26 of 26 leaves. The first is the branch that cleaves carbon–nitrogen bonds; the second has no counterpart in the published five-group scheme at all. Groups 1, 2, 3 and 4 do not: their largest single-group clade holds only 30–55 % of their members. The curated references alone behave the same way, so this is not an artefact of how variants were assigned — of those, the largest single-group clade holds 6 of 17 for group 1, 12 of 17 for group 2, 7 of 19 for group 3 and 3 of 11 for group 4. Across all 2,062 tips not even those 2 survive as clades, and for groups 2, 3, 4 and 5 the smallest clade containing every member is the whole tree. So read the colours as profile assignments that happen to cluster, not as a phylogeny that reproduces the group scheme. The measurement is downloadable, and the three sequence sets it uses are defined inside it. Tested again with bootstrap, because local support cannot answer this. The support values on the tree above are SH-like local support, which does not resample the alignment. A claim that a group is a clade needs the alignment columns resampled and the tree re-inferred, so that was done separately: 200 replicates on the 76 curated references, and 100 on the 530 sequences whose assignment is neither distant nor novel. Only one group survives as a clade among the references, and it survives convincingly: group 5 at 0.99. In the larger set group 5 is still the only group that forms a clade, but its support falls to 0.49 — the branch holds its shape while the evidence for it does not, which is exactly the distinction local support was hiding. The plant chlorophyll branch, the obvious candidate for a new group, is not a clade even among its own 3 references (2 of 3 in the largest single-group clade). Calling it a proposed group is not something this data supports. References bootstrap · Larger-set bootstrap

ROAR-DB, the Rieske Oxygenase Annotation Resource. Built from RefSeq and GenBank annotation with profile models of 76 Rieske oxygenases characterised in the literature. Every figure states its method and its limits; what the database cannot tell you is documented alongside what it can.
